fabian-strategy.s: A Fabian strategy is a military approach that avoids decisive pitched battles and instead wears down an enemy through attrition, delay and the destruction of supplies. It is named after the Roman general Quintus Fabius Maximus.

factionalism.s: Factionalism refers to the division of a ruling elite into rival groups whose struggles for power paralysed government and often led to civil war. It weakened many states, including the Mamluk Sultanate through rivalries among mamluk households, the Polish-Lithuanian…

fakir-azizuddin.s: Fakir Azizuddin was a Muslim physician and statesman who served as Ranjit Singh's principal foreign minister. He was the Sikh Empire's chief diplomatic interlocutor with the British, and his career illustrates the multireligious character of the Lahore Darbar.

fall-of-acre-1291.s: The fall of Acre in 1291 was the capture of the last major Crusader stronghold in the Levant by the Mamluk Sultanate. It effectively ended the Crusader states.

fall-of-beijing-1644.s: The fall of Beijing in 1644 was the capture of the Ming capital by the rebel army of Li Zicheng. The Chongzhen Emperor took his own life, ending the Ming Empire's rule over China.

fall-of-constantinople.s: The fall of Constantinople was the capture of the Byzantine capital by the Ottoman sultan Mehmed II in 1453, after a siege in which heavy artillery played a major role. It ended the Byzantine Empire and made the city the Ottoman capital.

fall-of-cordoba.s: The fall of Córdoba was the capture of the city by Ferdinand III of Castile in 1236. Once the capital of Umayyad al-Andalus, its loss followed the collapse of Almohad Caliphate power in Iberia after the Battle of Las Navas de Tolosa and was a major step in the Christian…

fall-of-granada.s: The fall of Granada was the surrender of the Nasrid kingdom of Granada, the last Muslim state in Iberia, to Ferdinand and Isabella in 1492. It completed the Christian reconquest of the peninsula, the final chapter in a process that had accelerated with the collapse of the…

fall-of-harran.s: The fall of Harran in 609 BCE was the defeat of the last Assyrian remnant, under Ashur-uballit II, by the Babylonians and their allies. It followed the destruction of Nineveh in 612 BCE and marked the final end of the Assyrian Empire.

fall-of-herat-1507.s: The fall of Herat in 1507 was the capture of the last Timurid capital by the Uzbek leader Muhammad Shaybani Khan. It ended Timurid rule in Khorasan and marked the end of the Timurid Empire, although the Timurid prince Babur later founded the Mughal Empire in India.

fall-of-nineveh.s: The fall of Nineveh was the destruction of the Assyrian capital in 612 BCE by a coalition of Medes and Babylonians. It was the decisive blow to the Assyrian Empire and a founding moment of Median power.

fall-of-oyo-ile.s: The fall of Oyo-Ile, around 1835–1836, was the abandonment of the capital of the Oyo Empire under pressure from the Ilorin emirate and the Sokoto Caliphate's expansion. The court relocated south to a new Oyo, and the old empire disintegrated into competing Yoruba states.

fall-of-seville.s: The fall of Seville was the capture of the city by Ferdinand III of Castile in 1248 after a long siege. Seville had been the Almohad Caliphate's main capital in al-Andalus, and its loss confirmed the end of Almohad power in the Iberian Peninsula.

fall-of-singapore.s: The fall of Singapore was the surrender of the British garrison to Japanese forces in February 1942, after a rapid campaign through Malaya. It was one of the greatest triumphs of the Empire of Japan in the Second World War and a severe blow to British imperial prestige in Asia.

fall-of-tenochtitlan.s: The fall of Tenochtitlan was the capture of the Aztec capital in 1521 by Spanish forces under Hernán Cortés and their indigenous allies, after a long siege worsened by a smallpox epidemic. It brought an end to the Aztec Empire and opened the Spanish conquest of Mexico.

fall-of-the-median-empire.s: The fall of the Median Empire took place in 550 BCE, when Cyrus the Great of Persia defeated the Median king Astyages, helped by the defection of part of the Median army, and captured Ecbatana. Media became a core part of the new Achaemenid Empire, and Medes continued to hold…

fall-of-the-western-roman-empire.n: Fall of the Western Roman Empire
fall-of-the-western-roman-empire.s: The fall of the Western Roman Empire is conventionally dated to 476 CE, when the Germanic commander Odoacer deposed the last western emperor, Romulus Augustulus. It was the culmination of a long period of invasion, civil war and fiscal decline, while the eastern half of the…

falun-mine.s: The Falun Mine was a copper mine in central Sweden, worked for many centuries. In the seventeenth century Sweden was the world's largest copper producer, and the Falun mine's output was for decades the largest single source of revenue for the Swedish Empire.

famine.s: Famine, a severe and widespread shortage of food, recurs throughout imperial history as a cause and consequence of political crisis. Often triggered by drought, war or failed harvests, it destroyed tax bases and provoked revolts.

fancheng.s: Fancheng was a city on the Han River in central China, paired with Xiangyang on the opposite bank. Together the twin cities guarded the route to the Yangtze valley, and their resistance during the Mongol siege of 1267–1273 was pivotal; their fall opened the way to the conquest…

farba.s: A farba was a provincial governor in the Mali Empire. Farbas exercised authority delegated by the mansa over provinces and subject areas, balancing imperial oversight with a large degree of local autonomy alongside village chiefs.

fari.s: Fari was the title of provincial governors in the Songhai Empire. Appointed by the ruler and typically loyal military commanders or members of the royal family, they were responsible for collecting taxes, keeping order and organising forced labour, reflecting the centralising…

fars.s: Fars is a province in south-western Iran, the historical heartland of the Persians. It was the homeland of the Sasanian dynasty, and later Shiraz in Fars served as the capital of the Zand Empire.

fascism.s: Fascism is an authoritarian nationalist ideology that arose in Italy after the First World War under Benito Mussolini. Fascist Italy sought to revive Roman imperial glory through expansion, conquering Ethiopia in 1935–1936 and building the short-lived Italian Empire, which…

fatawa-i-alamgiri.s: The Fatawa-i-Alamgiri is a compilation of Islamic law of the Hanafi school, prepared by scholars under the patronage of the Mughal emperor Aurangzeb in the late seventeenth century. It reflected Aurangzeb's emphasis on Islamic orthodoxy and served as a legal reference in the…

fatima.s: Fatima was the daughter of the Prophet Muhammad and wife of Ali. The Fatimid Caliphate took its name from her, as its Ismaili imam-caliphs claimed descent from her and Ali, a claim that was central to their religious legitimacy.

fatimid-caliphate.s: The Fatimid Caliphate was an Ismaili Shi'a caliphate founded in North Africa in 909 that conquered Egypt in 969 and founded Cairo. At its height it ruled North Africa, Egypt, Syria and the Hejaz and rivalled the Abbasids.

fatimid-capture-of-damascus.s: The Fatimid capture of Damascus in 978 brought the city under the control of the Fatimid Caliphate after years of conflict with local forces and rivals. Control of Damascus was important to Fatimid ambitions in Syria, though their hold on the region remained contested.

fatimid-conquest-of-egypt.s: The Fatimid conquest of Egypt in 969 CE was led by the general Jawhar al-Siqilli, who took the country with little resistance from the weakened Ikhshidid regime. The Fatimid Caliphate then founded Cairo as its new capital, making Egypt the centre of its power.

fatwa.s: A fatwa is a formal legal opinion issued by a qualified Islamic jurist. Yusuf ibn Tashfin of the Almoravid Empire obtained fatwas from Maliki jurists condemning the taifa kings of al-Andalus as insufficiently observant, which served as religious justification for deposing them…

fauj-i-ain.s: The Fauj-i-Ain was the regular standing army of the Sikh Empire, created by Ranjit Singh. Trained along European lines, partly by European officers, it combined disciplined infantry, artillery and cavalry and was the main engine of Sikh expansion.

faxian.s: Faxian was a Chinese Buddhist monk who travelled to India in search of Buddhist texts, staying there during 399–414 CE. His account of the journey describes the prosperity, peace and mild government of the Gupta Empire under Chandragupta II, making it a valuable outside source…

february-revolution.s: The February Revolution of 1917 was the uprising in Petrograd that forced the abdication of Tsar Nicholas II. It ended the Romanov monarchy and the Russian Empire, establishing a provisional government that was overthrown by the Bolsheviks later that year.

federalism.s: Federalism is a system of government in which power is divided between a central authority and constituent units. Proposals to federalise the Austro-Hungarian Empire were discussed as a way to satisfy its many nationalities but were never carried out.

feigned-retreat.s: The feigned retreat is a tactic in which an army pretends to flee in order to draw the enemy into breaking formation, then turns to attack. It was a hallmark of steppe warfare and was used with great effect by the Mongol Empire and its successor states, including the Chagatai…

ferdinand-ii-of-aragon.s: Ferdinand II of Aragon was king of Aragon whose marriage to Isabella of Castile united the two crowns. Together they completed the conquest of Granada in 1492, sponsored Columbus's voyage and expelled the Jews, laying the foundations of the Spanish Empire.

ferdinand-iii-of-castile.s: Ferdinand III was king of Castile and later León in the thirteenth century. Exploiting the collapse of the Almohad Caliphate in Spain, he conquered Córdoba in 1236 and Seville in 1248, among the greatest advances of the Christian reconquest.

ferenc-deak.s: Ferenc Deák was a Hungarian statesman who led the negotiations that produced the Compromise of 1867. The agreement created the Dual Monarchy, giving Hungary self-government within the Austro-Hungarian Empire, and he is often called the 'wise man of the nation'.

ferghana-valley.s: The Ferghana Valley is a fertile basin in Central Asia, today shared by Uzbekistan, Kyrgyzstan and Tajikistan. In the late second century BCE the Han Dynasty sent armies there to obtain its famous 'heavenly horses', extending Chinese influence into Central Asia.

fernando-alvarez-de-toledo-3rd-duke-of-a.n: Fernando Álvarez de Toledo, 3rd Duke of Alba
fernando-alvarez-de-toledo-3rd-duke-of-a.s: Fernando Álvarez de Toledo, 3rd Duke of Alba, was a Spanish general and statesman. As governor of the Netherlands from 1567 he carried out harsh repression of the Dutch revolt.

feudalism.s: Feudalism is a term for systems in which land was granted in return for military service and loyalty, creating hierarchies of lords and vassals. Originally applied to medieval Europe such as the Holy Roman Empire, it is used more loosely for comparable arrangements elsewhere,…

fez.s: Fez is a city in northern Morocco, founded in the late eighth century and long one of the major centres of Islamic learning and trade in the Maghreb. The Almoravid Empire conquered it during its expansion northward in the eleventh century, absorbing it into its realm.

fezzan.s: The Fezzan is a desert region of south-western Libya. It was the homeland of the Garamantian Empire, which developed foggara irrigation tunnels to tap underground water and controlled trans-Saharan trade.

field-artillery.s: Field artillery refers to mobile cannon used on the battlefield. Gunpowder artillery transformed warfare from the fifteenth century, giving decisive advantages to the Ottoman Empire and the Mughal Empire, whose cannon at Panipat helped defeat the Delhi Sultanate.

field-of-lies.s: The Field of Lies was the place near Colmar where, in 833 CE, the army of Emperor Louis the Pious deserted to his rebellious sons. Louis was deposed and publicly humiliated, though he was restored the following year.

fifth-syrian-war.s: The Fifth Syrian War, fought in 202–198 BCE, was a conflict between the Seleucid Empire under Antiochus III and the Ptolemaic kingdom. Antiochus's victory at Panium gave the Seleucids control of Coele-Syria, including Judea, ending a century of Ptolemaic rule there.

fin-de-siecle.s: Fin de siècle ('end of the century') refers to the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries, a period associated with cultural innovation and a sense of decadence. In Vienna, the capital of the Austro-Hungarian Empire, it saw an extraordinary flowering in psychoanalysis,…

finance-commission.s: The Finance Commission was one of the three councils at the centre of Song Dynasty government, alongside the Secretariat-Chancellery and the Bureau of Military Affairs. It managed state finances, and the overlapping jurisdiction of these councils was intended to prevent any…

finland.s: Finland is a country in northern Europe on the Baltic Sea. It was an integral part of the Swedish realm for centuries and supplied troops to the Swedish Empire.

finnic-peoples.s: The Finnic peoples are a group of Uralic-speaking peoples of northern Eastern Europe. Some Finnic and Slavic tribes paid tribute to the Khazar Khaganate, which drew revenue from its dominance over the peoples of the Volga and forest zones.

fire-arrow.s: A fire arrow was an arrow carrying an incendiary or gunpowder charge. The Song Dynasty developed and used gunpowder weapons, including fire arrows, bombs and early firearms, well before they appeared elsewhere, partly to compensate for its weakness against mounted nomadic armies.

fire-of-moscow-1812.s: The Fire of Moscow broke out in September 1812, shortly after Napoleon's army occupied the city. Much of Moscow was destroyed, depriving the French of shelter and supplies, and Napoleon was soon forced into a disastrous retreat.

fire-temple.s: A fire temple is a place of worship in Zoroastrianism, where a sacred fire is kept burning. Under the Sasanian Empire, Zoroastrianism was closely linked to the state, and great fire temples, some associated with the monarchy, were important religious and political centres.

first-anglo-sikh-war.s: The First Anglo-Sikh War was fought in 1845–1846 between the Sikh Empire and the British East India Company. The Khalsa army fought hard but was defeated, partly owing to the manoeuvres of its own leaders.

first-arab-siege-of-constantinople.s: The first Arab siege of Constantinople was a series of attacks on the Byzantine capital by the Umayyad Caliphate in 674–678. The city's walls and the Byzantine use of Greek fire defeated the assaults, and the failure checked Arab expansion into south-eastern Europe.

first-battle-of-panipat.s: The First Battle of Panipat was fought in 1526 between Babur and Ibrahim Lodi, the last sultan of Delhi. Babur's use of field artillery and cavalry tactics defeated a much larger army, ending the Delhi Sultanate and founding the Mughal Empire.

first-battle-of-the-marne.s: The First Battle of the Marne was fought in September 1914, when French and British forces halted the German advance towards Paris. It ended the German Empire's hopes of a quick victory in the west and led to the years of trench warfare on the Western Front.

first-chimurenga.s: The First Chimurenga was the uprising of the Ndebele and Shona against the British South Africa Company in 1896–1897, in what is now Zimbabwe. The Rozvi Empire profile notes that religious networks, notably the Mwari cult it had patronised, played a significant role in…

first-crusade.s: The First Crusade was a military expedition by western European Christians that captured Jerusalem in 1099 and established the Crusader states. It took Jerusalem from the Fatimid Caliphate, and the struggle against the Crusader states later shaped the rise of the Ayyubid…

first-fitna.s: The First Fitna was the first civil war within the Muslim community, fought in 656–661 CE after the assassination of Caliph Uthman. It pitted Caliph Ali against opponents including Mu'awiya, governor of Syria, and ended with Ali's assassination and Mu'awiya's founding of the…

first-italo-ethiopian-war.s: The First Italo-Ethiopian War was fought in 1895–1896 between Italy and the Ethiopian Empire under Menelik II. It ended with the crushing Italian defeat at the Battle of Adwa in 1896, which secured Ethiopian independence and was a major humiliation for the Italian Empire's…

first-opium-war.s: The First Opium War was fought in 1839–1842 between Britain and the Qing Empire, after Chinese efforts to suppress the opium trade. British naval superiority forced China to accept the Treaty of Nanjing, which ceded Hong Kong, opened ports to trade and began the era of unequal…

first-partition-of-poland.s: The First Partition of Poland in 1772 was the annexation of large parts of the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth by Russia, Prussia and Austria. It reduced the Commonwealth's territory and population substantially and began the process that ended with its complete disappearance…

first-punic-war.s: The First Punic War was fought in 264–241 BCE between Carthage and Rome, mainly over Sicily. Rome built a navy and won a decisive naval victory at the Aegates Islands, forcing Carthage to give up Sicily and pay an indemnity.

first-sino-japanese-war.s: The First Sino-Japanese War was fought in 1894–1895 between the Qing Empire and the Empire of Japan, mainly over control of Korea. Japan's modernised forces won decisively, and the Treaty of Shimonoseki gave Japan Taiwan and an indemnity, revealing Qing weakness and marking…

first-turkic-khaganate.s: The First Turkic Khaganate was the empire founded by the Ashina clan in 552 after the overthrow of the Rouran. It quickly extended across the Eurasian steppe from Manchuria to the Black Sea, before splitting into eastern and western khaganates.

first-world-war.s: The First World War (1914–1918) was a global conflict between the Allied Powers, including Britain, France and Russia, and the Central Powers, including Germany, Austria-Hungary and the Ottoman Empire. It destroyed the Austro-Hungarian, German, Russian and Ottoman Empires and…

fiscal-crisis.s: Fiscal crisis refers to a state's inability to raise enough revenue to meet its military and administrative costs, often leading to debasement, heavier taxation, unpaid troops and revolt. It was a recurring cause of decline, seen in the Spanish Empire's repeated bankruptcies,…

fiscal-military-state.s: The fiscal-military state is a concept describing states that developed efficient taxation, public borrowing and bureaucracy to finance large armed forces. Britain after 1688, with the Bank of England, the national debt and the Royal Navy, is the classic example, and this…

five-dynasties-and-ten-kingdoms-period.n: Five Dynasties and Ten Kingdoms period
five-dynasties-and-ten-kingdoms-period.s: The Five Dynasties and Ten Kingdoms period (907–979) was an era of political division in China after the fall of the Tang Dynasty. Short-lived dynasties succeeded one another in the north while several kingdoms ruled the south.

flanders.s: Flanders is a historic region in the southern Low Countries, now largely in Belgium. A wealthy centre of textile production and trade, it passed to the Habsburgs and formed part of the Spanish Empire's possessions in the Low Countries, where it was heavily affected by the wars…

flax.s: Flax is a plant grown for its fibres, which are made into linen, and for its seeds. Egypt's Nile valley supported intensive cultivation of cereals and flax under the Mamluk Sultanate, and linen production was an important part of the Egyptian economy.

floods-and-natural-disasters.s: Floods and natural disasters, such as river floods, failed Nile inundations and earthquakes, could devastate harvests, cities and state revenues. They contributed to the decline of the Yuan Dynasty, whose Yellow River floods sparked unrest, the Ming Empire, the Fatimid…

florence.s: Florence is a city in Tuscany, central Italy, and a leading centre of the Renaissance. Byzantine émigré scholars contributed greatly to the revival of Greek learning there, and the Council of Florence (1438–1445) sought to reunite the Byzantine and Latin churches in the last…

florentine-codex.s: The Florentine Codex is a sixteenth-century encyclopedic work on the Aztec world compiled by the Franciscan friar Bernardino de Sahagún with Nahua informants. Written in Nahuatl and Spanish and richly illustrated, it is one of the most important sources on the society,…

flower-wars.s: The Flower Wars were ritualised conflicts fought by the Aztec Empire with neighbouring states such as Tlaxcala. Their purpose is thought to have included training warriors and capturing prisoners for sacrifice rather than conquering territory.

foggara.s: A foggara is an underground irrigation tunnel that taps groundwater and carries it by gravity to the surface, similar to the Persian qanat. The Garamantian Empire built an extensive foggara network in the Fezzan from c.

folwark.s: A folwark was a large manorial farm in the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth, worked by serf labour and producing grain for export. The folwark system enriched the szlachta nobility through the Baltic grain trade but tied peasants more tightly to the land through heavy labour…

fortified-camp.s: A fortified camp is a defended encampment built by an army on campaign. Roman legions routinely constructed fortified camps as part of their engineering discipline, and under Idris Alooma the army of the Kanem-Bornu Empire adopted fortified camps as part of its military reforms.

four-estates-sasanian.s: The four estates were the social classes of the Sasanian Empire: priests, warriors, scribes and commoners such as peasants and artisans. This hierarchy, supported by Zoroastrian teaching, defined social status and duties and was a key part of Sasanian ideology.

four-class-system.s: The four-class system was the ethnic hierarchy of the Yuan Dynasty, ranking subjects as Mongols, semu (various Central and Western Asian peoples), Han (northern Chinese) and southerners. It determined access to office and legal treatment, and the resentment it caused…

fourteen-points.s: The Fourteen Points were a statement of principles for peace issued by US President Woodrow Wilson in 1918. They called for self-determination, including autonomous development for the peoples of Austria-Hungary, encouraging national movements that contributed to the break-up…

fourth-anglo-ashanti-war.s: The Fourth Anglo-Ashanti War of 1895–96 was a British expedition against the Ashanti Empire. Kumasi was occupied without major battle, the Asantehene Prempeh I was exiled to the Seychelles, and a British protectorate was imposed.

fourth-anglo-dutch-war.s: The Fourth Anglo-Dutch War was fought in 1780–1784 between Britain and the Dutch Republic, linked to Dutch trade with the American rebels. The Dutch suffered heavy losses of shipping and colonial trade, a blow that exposed and accelerated the decline of the Dutch Empire.

fourth-crusade.s: The Fourth Crusade was a Western expedition that, instead of reaching the Holy Land, sacked Constantinople in 1204. The crusaders established a Latin Empire, and although the Byzantines recovered the city in 1261, the Byzantine Empire never regained its former strength.

francafrique.s: Françafrique is a term for the close and often informal political, economic and military ties that France maintained with its former African colonies after independence. It reflects the lasting influence of the French Empire, including the role of French-educated elites in…

france.s: France is a country in western Europe that grew from the western part of the Carolingian Empire. It built the French Empire overseas and was a central actor in European power politics, appearing in the histories of empires from the Holy Roman Empire and the Ottoman Empire to…

francia.s: Francia was the realm of the Franks in western Europe, covering much of present-day France, the Low Countries and western Germany. It formed the heart of the Carolingian Empire, and its forces under Charles Martel halted the Umayyad Caliphate's advance at the Battle of Tours…

francis-i.s: Francis I was king of France from 1515 to 1547, a patron of the Renaissance and a rival of the Habsburg emperor Charles V. The voyages of Jacques Cartier to the Gulf of St Lawrence in 1534 were undertaken in his name, beginning French claims in North America that underlay the…

francis-ii.s: Francis II was the last Holy Roman Emperor. Faced with Napoleon's dominance, he proclaimed himself Emperor of Austria in 1804 and abdicated the Holy Roman imperial title in 1806, formally dissolving the Holy Roman Empire.

francisco-de-almeida.s: Francisco de Almeida was a Portuguese nobleman and the first viceroy of Portuguese India. He established fortified bases on the East African and Indian coasts and defeated a Mamluk and Gujarati fleet at the Battle of Diu in 1509, securing Portuguese naval dominance in the…

francisco-de-vitoria.s: Francisco de Vitoria was a Spanish Dominican theologian of the School of Salamanca. He questioned the legal justifications for the Spanish Empire's conquest of the Americas and argued that indigenous peoples had rights, and his work is regarded as a foundation of international…

francisco-pizarro.s: Francisco Pizarro was a Spanish conquistador who led the conquest of the Inca Empire. In 1532 he captured the Inca ruler Atahualpa at Cajamarca and later executed him, opening the way to Spanish control of Peru and enormous silver wealth for the Spanish Empire.

franco-mongol-alliance.s: The Franco-Mongol alliance refers to attempts in the thirteenth and early fourteenth centuries to coordinate action between the Mongol Ilkhanate and Christian European rulers and the papacy against the Mamluks. Embassies were exchanged, but the efforts never produced effective…

franco-prussian-war.s: The Franco-Prussian War of 1870–1871 was fought between France and a German coalition led by Prussia. The German victory led to the fall of Napoleon III, the annexation of Alsace-Lorraine and the proclamation of the German Empire at Versailles in January 1871.

frank-schwartz.s: Frank Schwartz is a geoscientist cited in the Garamantian Empire profile for a 2023 hydrological study. According to the site, his work showed that the Garamantes' foggara tunnels functioned only while the groundwater table stayed above the tunnel intakes, explaining how…

frankfurt.s: Frankfurt am Main is a city in western Germany. In the Holy Roman Empire it was a wealthy commercial centre and the traditional place where the emperors were elected, and later also crowned.

frankish-kingdom.s: The Frankish Kingdom was the realm of the Franks, a Germanic people who established power in Gaul after the fall of Rome, first under the Merovingian dynasty. Under the Carolingians it expanded into the Carolingian Empire, and its eastern part later became the core of the Holy…

franz-conrad-von-hotzendorf.s: Franz Conrad von Hötzendorf was Chief of the General Staff of the Austro-Hungarian army. He repeatedly urged preventive war against Serbia and Italy, and his aggressive offensive plans in 1914 exceeded the army's capabilities, contributing to heavy early losses for the…

franz-joseph-i.s: Franz Joseph I was Emperor of Austria and King of Hungary (r. 1848–1916).

frederic-hodgson.s: Frederic Hodgson was the British governor of the Gold Coast at the end of the nineteenth century. His demand in 1900 that the Golden Stool, the sacred symbol of the Ashanti Empire, be surrendered provoked the War of the Golden Stool led by Yaa Asantewaa.

frederick-barbarossa.s: Frederick Barbarossa was Holy Roman Emperor in the twelfth century. He sought to assert imperial authority in Germany and Italy, clashing with the papacy and the Lombard cities, and he drowned in 1190 while leading an army on the Third Crusade.

frederick-ii.s: Frederick II was Holy Roman Emperor and King of Sicily in the thirteenth century. Through the Treaty of Jaffa in 1229 he obtained Jerusalem from the Ayyubid sultan al-Kamil by negotiation, a concession that al-Kamil made for political support against his Ayyubid rivals.

frederick-lugard.s: Frederick Lugard was a British colonial administrator who became high commissioner of the Protectorate of Northern Nigeria in 1900. His forces conquered the emirates of the Sokoto Caliphate between 1900 and 1903, after which he governed through the existing emirs in a system…

free-imperial-city.s: A free imperial city was a city in the Holy Roman Empire that was subject only to the emperor rather than a territorial prince. Such cities had self-government and representation in the Imperial Diet.

freedmen.s: Freedmen were former slaves who had been granted their freedom. In the Roman Empire they formed a significant social group; they gained citizenship but faced some restrictions, and some became wealthy or held influential posts in the imperial household.

french-colonial-empire.s: The French colonial empire comprised the overseas territories ruled by France. The first empire, built from the seventeenth century in North America, the Caribbean and India, was largely lost by 1815; the second, built from the conquest of Algeria in 1830, covered large parts…

french-community.s: The French Community was an association created by de Gaulle's constitution of 1958 to replace the French Union, offering colonies autonomy within a French framework. Guinea immediately chose independence instead, and within a few years most African members became independent,…

french-conquest-of-bornu.s: The French conquest of Bornu in 1900 followed the defeat and death of the warlord Rabih az-Zubayr, who had seized Bornu in 1893. French control of the region accelerated the advance into the central Sahel and brought France into direct confrontation with the Wadai Empire.

french-east-india-company.s: The French East India Company was a chartered trading company founded in 1664 under Louis XIV's minister Colbert. It established posts in India, notably Pondicherry, and competed with the British East India Company, but lost out in the wars of the mid-eighteenth century,…

french-equatorial-africa.s: French Equatorial Africa was a federation of French colonies in Central Africa, including present-day Chad, the Central African Republic, Congo and Gabon. Wadai was incorporated into it after the French conquest, and it formed part of the French Empire until independence in 1960.

french-foreign-legion.s: The French Foreign Legion is a branch of the French army founded in 1831 for foreign volunteers. It served in the conquest of Algeria and in many other colonial campaigns, becoming one of the best-known military instruments of the French Empire.

french-invasion-of-algiers.s: The French invasion of Algiers took place in 1830, when a French expedition captured the city and overthrew the Ottoman-era regency. It began a long and violent conquest of Algeria, which became the centrepiece of the second French Empire.

french-invasion-of-russia.s: The French invasion of Russia was Napoleon's campaign of 1812, known in Russia as the Patriotic War. The Russian army retreated, fought at Borodino, and Moscow burned after its occupation; Napoleon's retreat in winter destroyed most of his army, a turning point that raised the…

french-language.s: French is a Romance language that developed from Latin in France. Spread through the French Empire's administration and education, it became the language of elites in many former colonies and remains an official language across much of Africa and elsewhere.

french-revolutionary-occupation-of-the-n.n: French revolutionary occupation of the Netherlands
french-revolutionary-occupation-of-the-n.s: The French revolutionary occupation of the Netherlands took place in 1795, when French armies overran the Dutch Republic and established the Batavian Republic. Britain then seized many Dutch colonies, and the VOC was dissolved, marking a major blow to the Dutch Empire.

french-revolutionary-wars.s: The French Revolutionary Wars (1792–1802) were fought between revolutionary France and coalitions of European powers. French victories led to the loss of German lands west of the Rhine and the reorganisation of the empire's territories, setting in motion the dissolution of the…

french-sahelian-mission.s: The French Sahelian Mission refers to the French military advance into the central Sahel in the early twentieth century. Sultan Doud Murra of the Wadai Empire resisted it, but the disparity in weapons proved decisive, and Wadai's independence ended with the French capture of…

french-union.s: The French Union was the political structure created in 1946 to replace the French colonial empire, theoretically making colonial subjects citizens with representation in Paris. It was applied inconsistently, satisfied few, and was replaced by the French Community in 1958.

french-wars-of-religion.s: The French Wars of Religion were a series of civil wars between Catholics and Protestants (Huguenots) in France in the second half of the sixteenth century. They ended with the Edict of Nantes in 1598.

frumentius.s: Frumentius was a Syrian Christian who, according to tradition, was brought to Aksum as a captive and rose to serve at the royal court. He helped bring Christianity to the Aksumite Empire under King Ezana and was consecrated the first bishop of Aksum by Athanasius of…

fubing-system.s: The fubing system was a militia system used in China from the Western Wei to the early Tang Dynasty, in which farming households provided soldiers in return for land. It supplied troops cheaply, but as frontier wars demanded permanent professional armies it broke down in the…

fugger-family.s: The Fugger family was a merchant and banking dynasty of Augsburg in the Holy Roman Empire. Grown wealthy from textiles, mining and finance in the fifteenth and sixteenth centuries, they lent heavily to the Habsburgs, notably financing Charles V's election as emperor in 1519.

fula.s: The Fula, also called Fulani, are a widely dispersed people of West and Central Africa, traditionally associated with cattle herding and Islamic scholarship. Fulani reformers led the jihad that created the Sokoto Caliphate, Fula states destroyed the Kaabu Empire at Kansala in…

fulani-war.s: The Fulani War, or Fulani jihad, of 1804–1810 was the Islamic reform movement led by Usman dan Fodio against the Hausa kingdoms. It created the Sokoto Caliphate, one of the largest states in nineteenth-century Africa, and its spread destabilised neighbours including the…

fundus.s: A fundus was a Roman landed estate or farm. In the Roman Empire small subsistence farms existed alongside large slave-worked estates (latifundia), and agriculture formed the economic backbone of the empire.

funj-sultanate-of-sennar.s: The Funj Sultanate of Sennar was a Muslim state on the Blue Nile in present-day Sudan, founded in the early sixteenth century. It was a neighbour and rival of the Darfur Sultanate, and the two contested Kordofan, before Sennar was conquered by Egypt in 1821.

fur-people.s: The Fur are a people of western Sudan whose homeland centres on the Jebel Marra highlands. They formed the core of the Darfur Sultanate, which takes its name from them ('Dar Fur', the land of the Fur), and their agriculture underpinned the state's economy.

fur-trade.s: The fur trade was the commerce in animal pelts, highly valued for clothing and as luxury goods. Furs from the northern forests passed through the Khazar Khaganate and the Black Sea to the Byzantine Empire, financed Russian Empire expansion across Siberia, and were central to…

fustat.s: Fustat was the first Arab capital of Egypt, founded by Amr ibn al-As around 641 during the Rashidun Caliphate's conquest. It became a major commercial city, and it remained an important centre after the Fatimid Caliphate founded Cairo nearby.

fyodor-dostoevsky.s: Fyodor Dostoevsky was a Russian novelist of the nineteenth century, author of Crime and Punishment and The Brothers Karamazov. He is cited as part of the literary and musical flowering of the Russian Empire, alongside Pushkin, Tolstoy and Tchaikovsky.

ferdinand-ii-holy-roman-emperor.s: Ferdinand II, Holy Roman Emperor, was the son of Archduke Charles II of Inner Austria and ruled from Graz before becoming emperor in 1619. A Jesuit-educated champion of the Counter-Reformation, he expelled Protestant preachers from Styria and his other lands.

ferdinand-ii-of-the-two-sicilies.n: Ferdinand II of the Two Sicilies
ferdinand-ii-of-the-two-sicilies.s: Ferdinand II of the Two Sicilies was the Bourbon king of Naples and Sicily from 1830 to 1859. He opened Italy's first railway, from Naples to Portici, in 1839.

federation-of-arab-emirates-of-the-south.n: Federation of Arab Emirates of the South
federation-of-arab-emirates-of-the-south.s: The Federation of Arab Emirates of the South was formed in 1959 under British sponsorship by six states of the Western Aden Protectorate, including Beihan, Dhala, Fadhli, Audhali, Lower Yafa and Upper Aulaqi. Other sultanates and sheikhdoms joined, and in 1962 it was renamed…

frederick-iii-holy-roman-emperor.s: Frederick III was a Habsburg duke of Inner Austria who became King of the Romans in 1440 and the last emperor crowned in Rome, in 1452. In 1453 he confirmed the forged Privilegium Maius, giving the Habsburgs the title of archduke.

frederick-iii-elector-palatine.s: Frederick III, Elector Palatine, called the Pious, came from the Palatinate-Simmern line and became elector in 1559. He made the Palatinate the first Calvinist state of the Empire and sponsored the Heidelberg Catechism of 1563.

frederick-iii-duke-of-holstein-gottorp.s: Frederick III, Duke of Holstein-Gottorp, ruled from 1616 to 1659 and kept a cultured Lutheran court at Gottorp. He founded Friedrichstadt in 1621 for Dutch Remonstrant refugees and sent the embassy to Russia and Persia described by Adam Olearius.

frederick-iii-of-denmark.s: Frederick III was king of Denmark and Norway from 1648 to 1670. His war with Sweden cost Denmark Scania and its other provinces east of the Sound in 1658, but he won fame defending Copenhagen during the Swedish siege.

frederick-iii-prince-of-salm-kyrburg.s: Frederick III, Prince of Salm-Kyrburg, was a German prince who lived mainly in Paris, where he built the Hôtel de Salm, now the Palace of the Legion of Honour. He sympathised with the early French Revolution but was arrested during the Terror and guillotined in July 1794.

ferdinand-i-holy-roman-emperor.s: Ferdinand I was the younger brother of Charles V, who gave him the Austrian lands in 1521. After Louis II died at Mohács in 1526 he was elected king of Bohemia and Hungary, and Croatian nobles chose him in 1527, founding the Habsburg Monarchy of Central Europe.

ferdinand-i-of-austria.s: Ferdinand I of Austria was emperor from 1835 to 1848, also king of Hungary, Bohemia and Illyria. Suffering from epilepsy, he left government to a regency council dominated by Metternich.

ferdinand-i-of-bulgaria.s: Ferdinand I of Bulgaria, a German prince of the Saxe-Coburg and Gotha family, was elected prince of Bulgaria in 1887. In 1908 he declared full independence from the Ottoman Empire and took the title of tsar.

ferdinand-i-of-romania.s: Ferdinand I of Romania, of the Hohenzollern-Sigmaringen family, succeeded his uncle Carol I in 1914. He took Romania into the First World War on the Allied side in 1916, against his family's sympathies.

ferdinand-i-of-leon.s: Ferdinand I, called the Great, was a son of Sancho III of Navarre who received the county of Castile and became king of León in 1037 after killing Bermudo III in battle. He made the taifas of Toledo, Zaragoza, Seville and Badajoz pay him tribute and took Coimbra in 1064.

francisco-morazan.s: Francisco Morazán was a Honduran general and Liberal leader who captured Guatemala City in 1829 and was president of the Federal Republic of Central America from 1830 to 1839. He tried to hold the federation together against Conservative revolts, but it broke up into separate…

fu-jian-337-385.s: Fu Jian was the Di ruler of the Former Qin from 357, served by the able minister Wang Meng. He conquered Former Yan, Former Liang and Dai, unifying northern China in 376.

fort-jesus.s: Fort Jesus is a fortress built by the Portuguese at Mombasa between 1593 and 1596 to guard their trade on the Swahili coast. Designed by the Italian architect Giovanni Battista Cairati, it changed hands repeatedly: Omani forces of the Ya'ariba dynasty took it in 1698 after a…

frederick-william-i-of-prussia.s: Frederick William I was King in Prussia from 1713 to 1740, known as the Soldier King. He cut court spending, reformed the finances and the bureaucracy through the General Directory, and roughly doubled the army to around 80,000 men, one of the largest in Europe for the size of…

frederick-william-duke-of-mecklenburg-sc.s: Frederick William was Duke of Mecklenburg-Schwerin from 1692 to 1713. When the Güstrow line of the House of Mecklenburg died out in 1695, he disputed its inheritance with his uncle Adolf Frederick.

frederick-william-elector-of-hesse.s: Frederick William I was the last Elector of Hesse, co-regent from 1831 and sole ruler from 1847 to 1866. His quarrel with the Hessian parliament over the constitution of 1831, pursued through his minister Hassenpflug, led to the crisis of 1850 that nearly brought war between…

frederick-william-duke-of-brunswick-wolf.s: Frederick William, Duke of Brunswick-Wolfenbüttel, known as the Black Duke, lost his lands when Napoleon absorbed them into the Kingdom of Westphalia in 1807. In 1809 he raised the Black Brunswickers, a volunteer corps in black uniforms, fought his way across Germany to the…

fatali-khan-of-quba.s: Fatali Khan was Khan of Quba from 1758 to 1789. Taking advantage of the break-up of Iranian power after Nader Shah, he seized Derbent in 1765 and made Baku, Javad, Shirvan and other khanates his dependencies, uniting much of the eastern Caucasus along the Caspian.

ferdinand-vii-of-spain.s: Ferdinand VII was King of Spain in 1808 and again from 1813 to 1833. Napoleon forced him and his father Charles IV to abdicate at Bayonne in 1808 and held him in France, while juntas in Spain and America governed in his name.

francisco-de-montejo-the-younger.s: Francisco de Montejo the Younger was a Spanish conquistador, son of the adelantado Francisco de Montejo. After his father's failed campaigns he led the decisive conquest of northern Yucatán, founding Campeche in 1540 and Mérida in 1542 on the site of the Maya city of T'ho.

faisal-ii-of-iraq.s: Faisal II was the last King of Iraq, succeeding his father Ghazi as a child in 1939, with his uncle Abd al-Ilah as regent until 1953. His governments, dominated by Nuri al-Said, were closely tied to Britain and joined the Baghdad Pact.

federation-of-rhodesia-and-nyasaland.s: The Federation of Rhodesia and Nyasaland, or Central African Federation, joined the British territories of Southern Rhodesia, Northern Rhodesia and Nyasaland from 1953 to 1963. Dominated by white settlers and governed from Salisbury, it faced strong African opposition.

felix-eboue.s: Félix Éboué was a French colonial administrator born in French Guiana, the first Black governor of a French colony. As governor of Chad he declared for Charles de Gaulle's Free France in August 1940, and most of French Equatorial Africa followed.

french-west-india-company.s: The French West India Company was a chartered company founded by Colbert in 1664 to run France's colonies and trade in the Americas and West Africa. It took over the French Caribbean islands, including Guadeloupe, Grenada and Saint Croix, and in 1665 appointed Bertrand…

faisal-ibn-turki-al-saud.s: Faisal ibn Turki Al Saud was imam of the Second Saudi State, the Emirate of Nejd, ruling from Riyadh in two reigns, 1834–1838 and 1843–1865. Between them an Egyptian expedition took him captive to Cairo, but he escaped and regained power.

faisal-bin-turki-sultan-of-muscat-and-om.n: Faisal bin Turki, Sultan of Muscat and Oman
faisal-bin-turki-sultan-of-muscat-and-om.s: Faisal bin Turki was Sultan of Muscat and Oman of the Al Said dynasty from 1888 until his death. His reign saw the sultanate fall further under British influence: his offer of a coaling station to France in 1898 was withdrawn under a British ultimatum.

fakhr-al-din-ii.s: Fakhr al-Din II was a Druze emir of the Ma'n family who governed the Shuf mountains and, as an Ottoman tax farmer, extended his authority over much of Lebanon, Galilee and the coast. After an Ottoman expedition against him he spent 1613–1618 in exile in Tuscany.

fayzulla-khodzhayev.s: Fayzulla Khodzhayev was the son of a wealthy Bukharan merchant and a leader of the Young Bukharan reform movement. After the Red Army stormed Bukhara in 1920 he headed the government of the Bukharan People's Soviet Republic, and from 1925 he chaired the Council of People's…

federal-charter-of-1291.s: The Federal Charter of 1291 is a Latin alliance document dated to early August 1291, in which the valley communities of Uri, Schwyz and Nidwalden promised each other aid against outside attack and agreed rules for keeping the peace and settling disputes. Rediscovered in the…

feltrino-gonzaga.s: Feltrino Gonzaga was a son of Luigi Gonzaga, the first Gonzaga lord of Mantua. He ruled Reggio Emilia as its lord from the 1330s until 1371, when he gave up the city to the Visconti of Milan, keeping only Novellara and Bagnolo in the plain to the north.

feng-ba.s: Feng Ba, known as Emperor Wencheng of Northern Yan, was a general of Han Chinese family in the service of Later Yan. In 407 he and Gao Yun killed the tyrannical emperor Murong Xi at Longcheng and made Gao Yun ruler.

first-nations-in-canada.s: First Nations is the name used for the Indigenous peoples of Canada other than the Inuit and Métis, made up of hundreds of distinct nations such as the Lekwungen, Nlaka'pamux and Tsilhqot'in of British Columbia. Colonial governments made land agreements with them, among them…

forbes-burnham.s: Forbes Burnham was a lawyer who co-founded the People's Progressive Party with Cheddi Jagan, then broke away to lead the People's National Congress, drawing support mainly from African Guyanese. He became premier of British Guiana in 1964 and led Guyana to independence in 1966.

fort-zeelandia-taiwan.s: Fort Zeelandia was the fortress built by the Dutch East India Company from 1624 at Tayouan, now Anping in Tainan, as the seat of government of Dutch Formosa. Koxinga besieged it in 1661, and in February 1662 its governor, Frederick Coyett, surrendered, ending Dutch rule on…

fort-zeelandia-guyana.s: Fort Zeelandia is a Dutch brick fort on Fort Island in the mouth of the Essequibo River in Guyana. Built in the 18th century, it replaced the older stronghold of Kyk-over-al as the seat of the Dutch colony of Essequibo, housing the commander and the colony's governing Court of…

francesco-sforza.s: Francesco Sforza was an Italian condottiere, son of Muzio Attendolo Sforza, who married Bianca Maria, daughter of Duke Filippo Maria Visconti of Milan. After the duke's death in 1447 he commanded the army of the Golden Ambrosian Republic, then turned against it and entered…

francis-xavier.s: Francis Xavier was a Navarrese priest and co-founder of the Society of Jesus who became the leading Catholic missionary in Asia. Based in Portuguese Goa from 1542, he preached in southern India, Malacca and the Moluccas, and in 1549 landed at Kagoshima, opening the Jesuit…

francisco-de-paula-santander.s: Francisco de Paula Santander was a New Granadan general of the wars of independence who fought beside Simón Bolívar at Boyacá in 1819. As vice-president of Gran Colombia he governed from Bogotá while Bolívar campaigned in the south, but the two fell out, and Santander was…

francisco-ramirez.s: Francisco Ramírez was a caudillo of Entre Ríos and a lieutenant of José Gervasio Artigas in the Federal League. With Estanislao López he defeated Buenos Aires at Cepeda in 1820 and signed the Treaty of Pilar, then turned on Artigas and drove him into exile.

franconian-circle.s: The Franconian Circle was one of the Imperial Circles into which the Holy Roman Empire was divided from 1500. It grouped the territories of Franconia, including the bishoprics of Bamberg, Würzburg and Eichstätt, the Hohenzollern margraviates, imperial cities such as Nuremberg…

frederick-augustus-duke-of-nassau.s: Frederick Augustus was prince of Nassau-Usingen from 1803 and, when it united with Nassau-Weilburg in 1806, the first duke of Nassau within Napoleon's Confederation of the Rhine. He shared government with his cousin Frederick William of Nassau-Weilburg, and the duchy kept its…

frederick-augustus-i-duke-of-oldenburg.n: Frederick Augustus I, Duke of Oldenburg
frederick-augustus-i-duke-of-oldenburg.s: Frederick Augustus of Holstein-Gottorp was prince-bishop of Lübeck and a kinsman of the Russian imperial family. Under the exchange agreed in the Treaty of Tsarskoye Selo, Grand Duke Paul of Russia passed the counties of Oldenburg and Delmenhorst to him in 1773, and the…

frederick-augustus-i-of-saxony.s: Frederick Augustus I was elector of Saxony from 1763 and became its first king in 1806 as an ally of Napoleon. The Treaty of Tilsit of 1807 also made him duke of Warsaw, a duchy he governed through ministers in Warsaw.

frederick-i-landgrave-of-hesse-homburg.s: Frederick I was the youngest son of Landgrave George I of Hesse-Darmstadt. In 1622 his brother Louis V granted him Homburg vor der Höhe as an appanage, making him the first landgrave of Hesse-Homburg, a branch that stayed dependent on Hesse-Darmstadt for most of its history.

frederick-i-of-wurttemberg.s: Frederick I was the last duke and first king of Württemberg. As an ally of Napoleon he became an elector in 1803 and king on 1 January 1806, nearly doubling his territory with church lands, imperial cities and Upper Swabia.

frederick-i-grand-duke-of-baden.n: Frederick I, Grand Duke of Baden
frederick-i-grand-duke-of-baden.s: Frederick I ruled Baden as regent from 1852 and as grand duke from 1856 until his death. Under him Baden became a liberal model state, with responsible ministers, religious toleration and civil equality for Jews.

frederick-i-duke-of-anhalt.s: Frederick I succeeded his father Leopold IV Frederick as duke of Anhalt in 1871 and reigned until his death. Anhalt had been reunited under his father in 1863, and under Frederick it was a member state of the new German Empire, governed from Dessau.

frederick-ii-of-denmark.s: Frederick II was king of Denmark and Norway from 1559. In his first year he bought the bishoprics of Ösel-Wiek and Courland for his younger brother Magnus of Holstein, drawing Denmark into the Livonian War.

frederick-the-great.s: Frederick the Great, Frederick II of Prussia, was king from 1740. That year he invaded Silesia, citing old Hohenzollern claims to duchies such as Brzeg and Krnov, and won most of it with the County of Kladsko in 1742.

frederick-william-i-duke-of-saxe-weimar.n: Frederick William I, Duke of Saxe-Weimar
frederick-william-i-duke-of-saxe-weimar.s: Frederick William I was a Saxon duke of the Ernestine line who received the lands around Weimar in the Erfurt Division of 1572. From 1591 to 1601 he also acted as regent of the Electorate of Saxony for the young elector Christian II.

frei-caneca.s: Frei Caneca, born Joaquim do Amor Divino Rabelo, was a Carmelite friar and journalist from Recife. He took part in the Pernambucan revolt of 1817 and was imprisoned until 1821.

french-revolution.s: The French Revolution was the period of upheaval in France that began with the meeting of the Estates-General in 1789, abolished the monarchy in 1792 and ended with Napoleon Bonaparte's seizure of power in 1799. Its ideas of popular sovereignty, equality and the rights of man…

friedrich-hildebrandt.s: Friedrich Hildebrandt was the Nazi Gauleiter of Mecklenburg who in 1933 became Reich governor of Mecklenburg-Schwerin and Mecklenburg-Strelitz, and from 1934 to 1945 of the merged Free State of Mecklenburg. An SS officer, he was tried after the war by an American military…

french-first-republic.s: The French First Republic was proclaimed in September 1792 after the overthrow of Louis XVI. Its armies fought the European monarchies in the French Revolutionary Wars and annexed the Austrian Netherlands, the left bank of the Rhine and small enclaves such as Salm, abolishing…

fa-ngum.s: Fa Ngum was the founder of Lan Xang, the first unified Lao kingdom. A prince of the Muang Sua ruling family raised in exile at the Khmer court of Angkor, he led an army up the Mekong with Khmer support and took Muang Sua in 1353.

faisal-i-of-iraq.s: Faisal I of Iraq was a son of Sharif Hussein of Mecca and a commander of the Arab Revolt against the Ottomans. In 1920 he was proclaimed king of the Arab Kingdom of Syria, but the French expelled him after the Battle of Maysalun.

faizullah-khan.s: Faizullah Khan was a Rohilla Afghan chief, son of Ali Muhammad Khan, who founded the princely state of Rampur. After the Nawab of Awadh and the British defeated the Rohillas in 1774, the Treaty of Lal Dhang let him keep Rampur and its surrounding lands.

fakhr-al-dawla-hasan.s: Fakhr al-Dawla Hasan was the last ruler of the Bavand dynasty, which had governed parts of Mazandaran in northern Iran since the 7th century. He ruled from Amol in the troubled years after the collapse of the Ilkhanate.

faroe-islands.s: The Faroe Islands are an archipelago in the North Atlantic between Shetland and Iceland, settled by Norse farmers in the 9th century. Their assembly at Tinganes in Tórshavn is one of the oldest in Europe.

fascist-italy.s: Fascist Italy was the Kingdom of Italy under the dictatorship of Benito Mussolini, from his appointment as prime minister in 1922 to his fall in 1943. The regime suppressed opposition, reconquered Libya, invaded Ethiopia in 1935 and aided Franco in the Spanish Civil War.

fath-ali-khan-afshar.s: Fath Ali Khan Afshar was the khan of Urmia and a leading contender for power in north-western Iran after the death of Nader Shah in 1747. He fought Azad Khan Afghan and the Qajar Mohammad Hasan Khan and for a time controlled much of Azerbaijan.

fath-ali-shah-qajar.s: Fath-Ali Shah Qajar was the second Qajar shah of Iran, reigning from 1797 to 1834 after his uncle Agha Mohammad Khan. His reign saw two wars with Russia, ended by the treaties of Gulistan in 1813 and Turkmenchay in 1828, which cost Iran its Caucasian lands.

fatherland-front-bulgaria.s: The Fatherland Front was a Bulgarian political coalition formed in 1942 under communist leadership to oppose the pro-German government. It seized power in a coup on 9 September 1944 as the Soviet army entered Bulgaria.

fatherland-front-austria.s: The Fatherland Front was the single ruling party of the authoritarian Federal State of Austria, founded by Chancellor Engelbert Dollfuss in 1933 after he suspended parliament. Drawing on Catholic corporatism and Italian Fascism, it replaced all other parties and opposed both…

faustin-soulouque.s: Faustin Soulouque was a Haitian general chosen president by the senate in 1847 as a supposedly pliable figure. He purged the mixed-race elite, proclaimed himself Emperor Faustin I in 1849 and built a lavish court.

federico-da-montefeltro.s: Federico da Montefeltro was lord of Urbino from 1444 and its first duke from 1474, and one of the most successful condottieri of Renaissance Italy. Fighting for Florence, the papacy and Naples, he sacked Volterra for Florence in 1472.

feng-hong.s: Feng Hong was the last ruler of the Northern Yan state in the Liaoxi region, seizing power in 430 after killing many of his brother Feng Ba's sons. Besieged by the Northern Wei, he fled in 436 to Goguryeo, which received him but grew wary of his ambitions.

ferdinando-carlo-gonzaga.s: Ferdinando Carlo Gonzaga was the last Gonzaga Duke of Mantua and Montferrat, ruling from 1665. A pleasure-loving and extravagant prince, he sold Casale to France and sided with Louis XIV in the War of the Spanish Succession.

fergus-mor.s: Fergus Mór mac Eirc was a legendary king of Dál Riata who, according to later tradition, moved the dynasty's seat from County Antrim to Argyll around 500. The kings of Dál Riata and the later kings of Scots traced their descent from him.

fernan-gonzalez-of-castile.s: Fernán González was Count of Castile from about 931 to 970. He united the counties of Castile, Álava and Lantarón under his rule and made Castile largely autonomous from the kings of León.

first-balkan-war.s: The First Balkan War was fought from October 1912 to May 1913 by the Balkan League of Bulgaria, Serbia, Greece and Montenegro against the Ottoman Empire. The allies took almost all Ottoman lands in Europe, including Macedonia, Thrace and Albania, and Albania declared…

first-sacred-war.s: The First Sacred War was fought in the early 6th century BCE by the Amphictyonic League, with Thessaly, Sicyon under Cleisthenes and Athens, against the town of Kirrha, accused of abusing pilgrims to Delphi. Kirrha was destroyed and its plain dedicated to Apollo.

firth-of-forth.s: The Firth of Forth is the estuary of the River Forth on the east coast of Scotland, with Edinburgh on its southern shore and Fife to the north. In Roman and early medieval times it marked a frontier zone between the Votadini and Gododdin to the south and the Picts to the north.

firuz-shah-tughluq.s: Firuz Shah Tughluq was Sultan of Delhi from 1351 to 1388. He led two unsuccessful invasions of Bengal and a costly campaign against the Samma rulers of Sindh, but otherwise preferred building to conquest, founding towns, canals and the citadel of Firozabad at Delhi.

fort-nassau-berbice.s: Fort Nassau was the Dutch fort and trading post on the Berbice River in present-day Guyana, about 90 km upstream, and the first seat of the Berbice colony founded by the van Peere family in 1627. It was the centre of the colony until the Berbice slave uprising of 1763, after…

fort-nassau-gold-coast.s: Fort Nassau was the first Dutch fort on the Gold Coast, built in 1612 at Moree in present-day Ghana at the invitation of the kingdom of Asebu. It served as Dutch headquarters on the coast until they captured Elmina from the Portuguese in 1637.

four-garrisons-of-anxi.s: The Four Garrisons of Anxi were Tang dynasty military posts in the Tarim Basin, usually Kucha, Khotan, Kashgar and Karasahr, under the Protectorate General to Pacify the West. They secured Chinese control of the Silk Road oasis kingdoms, which kept their own rulers, and were…

francis-light.s: Francis Light was a British trader and naval officer who founded the British settlement on Penang in 1786. He obtained the island from Sultan Abdullah of Kedah on behalf of the East India Company, implying military protection that the company never gave.

francisco-de-miranda.s: Francisco de Miranda was a Venezuelan revolutionary who served in the American and French revolutionary wars. His invasion of Venezuela in 1806 failed, but he returned in 1810 and pressed the congress to declare independence in 1811.

francisco-franco.s: Francisco Franco was a Spanish general who rose in the colonial wars in Morocco. In July 1936 he led the Army of Africa in the military rising against the Second Republic and was named head of state of the Nationalist side.

francisco-xavier-de-mendonca-furtado.s: Francisco Xavier de Mendonça Furtado was a Portuguese administrator, brother of the Marquis of Pombal, who governed the State of Grão-Pará and Maranhão from 1751 to 1759. He led the demarcation of the Amazon borders under the Treaty of Madrid, curtailed the Jesuit missions and…

frank-swettenham.s: Frank Swettenham was a British colonial administrator in Malaya. Fluent in Malay, he served as Resident of Selangor and Perak and, in 1896, became the first Resident-General of the Federated Malay States, which he had helped design.

frankfurt-parliament.s: The Frankfurt Parliament was the first freely elected all-German assembly, meeting in St Paul's Church in Frankfurt from May 1848 during the revolutions of that year. It drafted a liberal constitution for a united Germany and offered the imperial crown to Frederick William IV…

frederick-margrave-of-brandenburg-bayreu.s: Frederick was Margrave of Brandenburg-Bayreuth from 1735 to 1763 and husband of Wilhelmine, sister of Frederick the Great. Together they made Bayreuth a centre of art and music, building the Margravial Opera House, now a UNESCO World Heritage Site, and new palaces.

frederick-duke-of-saxe-altenburg.s: Frederick was Duke of Saxe-Hildburghausen from 1780 and, after the Ernestine lands were rearranged in 1826, the first Duke of the new Saxe-Altenburg. His daughter Therese married Crown Prince Ludwig of Bavaria in 1810, and the horse race held to celebrate the wedding in Munich…

frederick-seymour.s: Frederick Seymour was a British colonial official who succeeded James Douglas as governor of the mainland Colony of British Columbia in 1864. After the colony was merged with Vancouver Island in 1866 he governed the united Colony of British Columbia, at a time of heavy debt…

frederick-william-elector-of-brandenburg.s: Frederick William, Elector of Brandenburg, known as the Great Elector, ruled Brandenburg-Prussia from 1640. At the Peace of Westphalia in 1648 he gained the secularised bishoprics of Halberstadt and Minden and the reversion of Magdeburg, which passed to him in 1680.

french-antilles.s: The French Antilles are the islands of the Caribbean colonised by France from the 1620s, beginning with Saint Kitts and spreading to Guadeloupe, Martinique and smaller islands. In the 17th century a governor-general, most famously Philippe de Longvilliers de Poincy, oversaw…

friedrich-august-prince-of-anhalt-zerbst.s: Friedrich August, Prince of Anhalt-Zerbst, was the last ruler of the small German principality and the brother of Catherine the Great of Russia. He lived mostly abroad and hired out soldiers to Britain during the American Revolutionary War.

fulgencio-batista.s: Fulgencio Batista was a Cuban army sergeant who rose to power after the revolution of 1933 and dominated Cuban politics for most of the next quarter-century. He was elected president in 1940 and seized power again in a coup in 1952.

franz-von-waldeck.s: Franz von Waldeck was Prince-Bishop of Münster from 1532, and also of Minden and Osnabrück. When radical Anabaptists seized the city of Münster in 1534, he besieged it with help from neighbouring princes, and his forces took it in June 1535, ending the Anabaptist kingdom of…

filipe-de-brito-e-nicote.s: Filipe de Brito e Nicote was a Portuguese adventurer in the service of the king of Mrauk U who was put in charge of the port of Syriam, near present-day Yangon, after 1599. He made himself its independent ruler with support from Portuguese Goa, controlling the trade of lower…

fuad-stephens.s: Fuad Stephens, born Donald Stephens, was a journalist and Kadazan leader in North Borneo who founded the United National Kadazan Organisation. He helped bring the colony into Malaysia in 1963 as the state of Sabah and served as its first chief minister.

frederick-i-duke-of-wurttemberg.s: Frederick I, Duke of Württemberg, ruled the County of Montbéliard from 1581 and inherited the Duchy of Württemberg in 1593. A Lutheran prince with wide interests, he employed the architect Heinrich Schickhardt, who rebuilt much of Montbéliard and founded the new town of…

frederick-ii-of-legnica.s: Frederick II of Legnica was a Silesian Piast duke who ruled Legnica and from 1521 also Brzeg. He introduced the Lutheran Reformation to his duchies in the 1520s and founded a short-lived Protestant university at Legnica.

frederick-iv-duke-of-austria.s: Frederick IV, Duke of Austria, of the Habsburg dynasty, ruled Tyrol and the Habsburg lands in Further Austria. In 1415 he helped the antipope John XXIII flee the Council of Constance, and King Sigismund outlawed him.

frederick-iv-duke-of-saxe-gotha-altenbur.s: Frederick IV, Duke of Saxe-Gotha-Altenburg, was the last ruler of his line, succeeding his brother Augustus in 1822. Unmarried and in poor health, he died in 1825, and the extinction of the house led to the Ernestine redistribution of 1826, in which Gotha passed to Saxe-Coburg…

frederick-i-elector-of-brandenburg.s: Frederick I, Elector of Brandenburg, was a Hohenzollern burgrave of Nuremberg who supported Sigismund's election as king. In return he received the Margraviate of Brandenburg in 1415 and was invested as elector in 1417.

frederick-i-elector-palatine.s: Frederick I, Elector Palatine, called the Victorious, governed the Palatinate from 1451 as guardian of his nephew and then as elector in his own right. He defeated a coalition of neighbouring princes at Seckenheim in 1462.

frederick-i-of-prussia.s: Frederick I of Prussia succeeded as Elector Frederick III of Brandenburg in 1688. In 1701, with the emperor's consent, he crowned himself King in Prussia at Königsberg, raising the status of the Hohenzollern lands.

ferdinand-iii-holy-roman-emperor.s: Ferdinand III, Holy Roman Emperor, of the Habsburg dynasty, reigned from 1637 to 1657. He commanded the imperial army at Nördlingen in 1634 and, as emperor, sought to end the Thirty Years' War, accepting the Peace of Westphalia in 1648.

fada-ngourma.s: Fada N'Gourma is a town in eastern Burkina Faso and the historic capital of the Gulmanceba kingdom of Gulmu. Its king, the Bado, presided over provincial chiefs drawn from royal lineages.

fadl-ibn-rabia.s: Fadl ibn Rabi'a was a Bedouin emir of the Jarrahid family in Syria in the early 12th century. He shifted his allegiance between the Crusaders, the Seljuks and the Fatimids as circumstances changed, keeping his tribe's power on the desert fringe.

faiz-talab-khan.s: Faiz Talab Khan was a Pathan of the Barech tribe who served the British East India Company in the Second Anglo-Maratha War. In 1804 the British rewarded him with the district of Pataudi, near Delhi, making him the first Nawab of Pataudi State.

fakhr-al-mulk-ibn-ammar.s: Fakhr al-Mulk ibn Ammar was the last ruler of Tripoli in Lebanon from the Banu Ammar family of qadis, governing from 1099. He resisted the Crusader siege begun by Raymond of Saint-Gilles from his castle on Mount Pilgrim.

fakhruddin-mubarak-shah.s: Fakhruddin Mubarak Shah was the founder of the Sonargaon Sultanate in eastern Bengal. An armour-bearer of the Tughluq governor of Sonargaon, he seized power on his master's death in 1338 and declared independence from Muhammad bin Tughluq, the first ruler in Bengal to break…

famagan-wattara.s: Famagan Wattara was a Dyula warrior leader of the Wattara family of Kong and a kinsman of Seku Wattara, the founder of the Kong Empire. Around 1714 he led warriors into the upper Black Volta region and established the Kingdom of Gwiriko, ruling over the Bobo and other peoples…

fan-shiman.s: Fan Shiman was a king of Funan in the early 3rd century, known from Chinese histories. A general who was raised to the throne, he is said to have built a fleet and subdued more than ten neighbouring states, extending Funan's control over the coasts and trade routes of the Gulf…

fanum-voltumnae.s: Fanum Voltumnae, the shrine of Voltumna, was the federal sanctuary of the twelve peoples of Etruria, where their delegates met each year for games, sacrifices and council. Roman writers such as Livy place it in the territory of Volsinii.

farrukh-shah.s: Farrukh Shah was an Ayyubid prince, a nephew of Saladin, who received Baalbek as his fief in 1179 and served as his uncle's deputy in Damascus. He campaigned against the Crusader Kingdom of Jerusalem, raiding Galilee and the lands east of the Jordan.

farrukhan-the-great.s: Farrukhan the Great was the ispahbad of Tabaristan, the mountainous Caspian province of northern Iran, and the most powerful ruler of the Dabuyid dynasty. In 717 he defeated the invading army of the Umayyad general Yazid ibn al-Muhallab in the forests of the Alborz, forcing a…

fatali-khan-khoyski.s: Fatali Khan Khoyski was an Azerbaijani lawyer and politician who served as the first prime minister of the Azerbaijan Democratic Republic from May 1918 to 1919. His governments moved the capital to Baku, built state institutions and defended the republic's independence.

fateh-shah-of-garhwal.s: Fateh Shah was Raja of the Garhwal Kingdom in the Himalayan foothills in the late 17th and early 18th centuries. He kept a lively court at Srinagar in Garhwal, where painting and poetry flourished.

fateh-singh-ahluwalia.s: Fateh Singh Ahluwalia was the Sikh ruler of Kapurthala and head of the Ahluwalia misl from 1801 until his death. He was a close ally of Ranjit Singh, exchanging turbans with him as a sign of brotherhood and fighting in his campaigns that built the Sikh Empire.

fatehsinh-bhonsle.s: Fatehsinh Bhonsle was the founder of the Akkalkot State in the Deccan. Born into the Lokhande family, he was adopted as a boy by the Maratha king Shahu, who granted him Akkalkot in 1708.

fathullah-imad-ul-mulk.s: Fathullah Imad-ul-Mulk was the founder of the Imad Shahi dynasty of Berar. Born a Hindu in the lands of Vijayanagara, he was captured as a boy, converted to Islam and rose in Bahmani service to become governor of Berar.

fatima-soltan.s: Fatima Soltan was the last ruler of the Qasim Khanate, the Tatar vassal state of Muscovy centred on the town of Kasimov on the Oka. She was the widow of Khan Arslan Ali and the mother of Seyid Burhan.

federal-pact.s: The Federal Pact was an alliance signed in January 1831 by the Argentine provinces of Buenos Aires, Santa Fe and Entre Ríos against the Unitarian League of General José María Paz. After Paz was captured and the Unitarians defeated, the other provinces joined it.

federico-ii-gonzaga-duke-of-mantua.n: Federico II Gonzaga, Duke of Mantua
federico-ii-gonzaga-duke-of-mantua.s: Federico II Gonzaga, son of Isabella d'Este, ruled Mantua from 1519 and was raised from marquis to duke by Charles V in 1530. Through his marriage to Margherita Paleologa he acquired the Marquisate of Montferrat in 1536.

felek-al-din-dundar-bey.s: Felek al-Din Dundar Bey was the founder of the Hamidid beylik in the Lakes Region of south-western Anatolia, a grandson of Hamid Bey, a Turkmen commander of the Seljuks. As Seljuk power collapsed in the early 14th century he made himself ruler of Eğirdir and Isparta.

felice-baciocchi.s: Felice Baciocchi was a Corsican army officer who married Napoleon's sister Elisa Bonaparte in 1797. In 1805 Napoleon made the couple Princes of Lucca and Piombino, but Elisa held real power and Felice mostly commanded troops.

felipe-vi-of-spain.s: Felipe VI is King of Spain, succeeding on the abdication of his father Juan Carlos I in June 2014. As head of state of the parliamentary monarchy, he made a televised address in October 2017 condemning the unilateral independence referendum held by the Catalan government, the…

felix-gouin.s: Félix Gouin was a French Socialist politician who succeeded Charles de Gaulle as head of the Provisional Government of the French Republic in January 1946, serving until June. A lawyer who had refused full powers to Pétain in 1940, he oversaw the first draft constitution,…

ferchar-fota.s: Ferchar Fota, 'the Tall', was a king of Cenél Loairn in northern Argyll who in the late 7th century also held the kingship of Dál Riata, displacing the rival Cenél nGabráin. He is recorded in the Irish annals, which date his death to 697.

ferdinand-magellan.s: Ferdinand Magellan was a Portuguese navigator who led a Spanish expedition from 1519 to find a western route to the Spice Islands. He passed the strait that bears his name and crossed the Pacific, reaching the Philippines in 1521, where he met local rulers and was killed at…

ferdinand-marcos.s: Ferdinand Marcos was President of the Philippines from 1965 to 1986. He declared martial law in 1972 and ruled as a dictator, jailing opponents and enriching his family and cronies on a vast scale.

ferdinand-iii-grand-duke-of-tuscany.n: Ferdinand III, Grand Duke of Tuscany
ferdinand-iii-grand-duke-of-tuscany.s: Ferdinand III, Grand Duke of Tuscany, was a Habsburg prince who lost Tuscany to the French in 1799. In compensation he was given the secularised Archbishopric of Salzburg as an electorate in 1803, then exchanged it in 1805 for the Grand Duchy of Würzburg, which he ruled until…

ferdinand-von-furstenberg.s: Ferdinand von Fürstenberg was Prince-Bishop of Paderborn from 1661 and also of Münster from 1678. A learned humanist and Latin poet who had served at the papal court, he wrote the Monumenta Paderbornensia on the history of his diocese, supported scholars and missions in…

ferdinando-martini.s: Ferdinando Martini was an Italian writer and politician who served as the first civilian governor of Eritrea from 1897 to 1907, after Italy's defeat at Adwa. He moved the capital from Massawa to Asmara, reorganised the administration and reduced military rule, and kept a diary…

ferenc-nagy.s: Ferenc Nagy was a leader of the Independent Smallholders' Party who served as Prime Minister of Hungary from February 1946 to May 1947, during the short-lived Second Hungarian Republic. The Communists, backed by the Soviet occupation, broke up his party through arrests and…

ferenc-szalasi.s: Ferenc Szálasi was the leader of the fascist Arrow Cross Party, installed by Germany as head of the Hungarian state in October 1944 after Regent Miklós Horthy tried to leave the war. Ruling as Leader of the Nation, he kept Hungary fighting while his militias murdered thousands…

fergus-of-galloway.s: Fergus of Galloway was the first known Lord of Galloway in south-west Scotland, rising to power in the early 12th century and styled king in some sources. He married an illegitimate daughter of Henry I of England, founded religious houses such as Soulseat and Whithorn Priory,…

fernmail.s: Fernmail was a ruler of Buellt and Gwrtheyrnion in mid-Wales, named in the Historia Brittonum of about 829 as the king of those lands in the author's own day. The text traces his descent from Pascent, son of Vortigern, to whom Ambrosius was said to have granted the territories.

ferrante-i-gonzaga.s: Ferrante I Gonzaga was a son of Isabella d'Este and a leading general of the Emperor Charles V, serving as Viceroy of Sicily and from 1546 as governor of the Duchy of Milan. In 1539 he bought the county of Guastalla from Countess Ludovica Torelli, founding the Gonzaga line…

ferrante-gonzaga-marquis-of-castiglione.s: Ferrante Gonzaga was lord of Castiglione delle Stiviere, south of Lake Garda, from a cadet branch of the Gonzaga of Mantua. The emperor made him marquis in 1579.

fidel-castro.s: Fidel Castro was a Cuban revolutionary who led the 26th of July Movement against the dictatorship of Fulgencio Batista, attacking the Moncada barracks in 1953 and waging guerrilla war from the Sierra Maestra after 1956. He took power in January 1959, aligned Cuba with the…

filocalo-navigajoso.s: Filocalo Navigajoso was a Venetian noble who seized the Aegean island of Lemnos around 1207, during the Latin division of Byzantine lands after the Fourth Crusade. The Latin emperor named him megadux, grand admiral of the Latin Empire, a title his descendants kept.

firozpur-jhirka.s: Firozpur Jhirka is a town in the Mewat region south of Delhi, now in Haryana. In 1806 the British granted it to Ahmad Bakhsh Khan, the founder of Loharu State, as a reward for his service in the war of 1803.

first-anglo-afghan-war.s: The First Anglo-Afghan War was fought between the British East India Company and Afghanistan. In 1839 a British army, marching through Sindh, invaded, deposed Dost Mohammad Khan and installed Shah Shuja.

first-anglo-burmese-war.s: The First Anglo-Burmese War was fought between the British East India Company and the Konbaung kingdom of Burma, which had conquered Arakan, Assam and Manipur and pressed on British Bengal. After costly campaigns and the capture of Rangoon, the Treaty of Yandabo in 1826 forced…

first-carib-war.s: The First Carib War was fought on Saint Vincent between British forces and the Garifuna, or Black Caribs, who resisted British surveyors dividing their land into plantations after the island was ceded to Britain in 1763. Unable to defeat them in the mountainous north, the…

first-indochina-war.s: The First Indochina War was fought between France and the Viet Minh, led by Ho Chi Minh, after France tried to restore its rule over Indochina following the Second World War. The Viet Minh, aided from 1950 by China, defeated the French at Dien Bien Phu in 1954.

first-intermediate-period.s: The First Intermediate Period is the era of ancient Egyptian history between the collapse of the Old Kingdom and the reunification of the country in the Middle Kingdom. Royal authority at Memphis faded after the Sixth Dynasty, and power passed to provincial governors and rival…

first-nagorno-karabakh-war.s: The First Nagorno-Karabakh War was fought between Azerbaijan and Armenian forces over Nagorno-Karabakh, an Armenian-majority region of Soviet Azerbaijan, as the Soviet Union collapsed. Armenian forces took the region and seven surrounding districts, and hundreds of thousands…

first-macedonian-war.s: The First Macedonian War was fought between Rome and Philip V of Macedon, who had allied with Hannibal during the Second Punic War. Rome left most of the fighting to its Greek allies of the Aetolian League, while Roman fleets raided the coasts, sacking Dyme in 208 BCE.

first-samnite-war.s: The First Samnite War was the first conflict between Rome and the Samnites of the central Apennines. It began in 343 BCE when the Samnites attacked the Sidicini and then Capua, which appealed to Rome.

floriano-peixoto.s: Floriano Peixoto was a Brazilian army marshal who served as the second President of Brazil from 1891 to 1894, taking over when Deodoro da Fonseca resigned. Known as the Iron Marshal, he crushed the Federalist Revolution in the south and a naval revolt in Rio de Janeiro,…

fort-christina.s: Fort Christina was the first Swedish settlement in North America, built in 1638 by an expedition under Peter Minuit on the Christina River, at what is now Wilmington, Delaware, and named after Queen Christina. It was the centre of New Sweden until the colony surrendered to New…

fort-coligny.s: Fort Coligny was the stronghold of France Antarctique, built in 1555 by Nicolas Durand de Villegaignon on Serigipe island in Guanabara Bay, Brazil, and named after Admiral Gaspard de Coligny, the colony's patron. It sheltered French Catholics and Protestants allied with the…

fort-dansborg.s: Fort Dansborg is a Danish fort at Tranquebar, now Tharangambadi, on the Coromandel coast of Tamil Nadu, built in 1620 by Ove Gjedde on land granted by the Nayak of Thanjavur. It was the seat of the Danish governors and the centre of Denmark's Asian trade for over two…

fort-orange.s: Fort Orange was a Dutch fur-trading post built in 1624 by the Dutch West India Company on the upper Hudson River, at what is now Albany, New York. It was the main point of trade between New Netherland and the Mohawk and other Iroquois nations, who exchanged beaver pelts for…

fort-oranje-sint-eustatius.s: Fort Oranje is a fort above the harbour of Oranjestad on Sint Eustatius, built by Zeeland settlers from 1636.
